newsitem.title: USA: Quick action can curb drug-resistant TB - study.
newsitem.headline: Quick action can curb drug-resistant TB - study.

text.p: Drug-resistant tuberculosis is often fatal and can be spread inside hospitals, but quick diagnosis and proper treatment can extend lives, researchers said on Tuesday.
The finding from the New York City Department of Public Health was based on a review of 267 TB patients in that city over a 43-month period beginning in 1990.

Of these patients, 86 percent were infected with the virus that causes AIDS and 70 percent of the 267 cases were probably acquired in hospitals from patients who were already infected, the study said. Of the 267, 83 percent died over the course of the study period.

The fatalities could be reduced, the study said, through prompt diagnosis, closely watched treatment with remaining drugs that may be effective and isolating TB patients from those with immune problems.
The researchers said their data indicated proper treatment added from two or three months to a year to the lives of persons with damaged immune systems who suffered from drug-resistant TB.

The study was published in this week's Journal of the American Medical Association along with a related one from New York's Columbia University that tracked 229 new TB cases in New York City in 1991. That study found that 27 percent of the victims died within one year and mortality exceeded 44 percent after 3 1/2 years.
Some strains of TB have become resistant to the most commonly used drugs -- isoniazid and rifampin -- and are often fatal even though some alternative treatments are available.

A lengthy decline in TB cases in the United States was reversed during the 1980s. Experts blame the reverse on the AIDS epidemic, increasing poverty, more immigration and a dismantling of control procedures accompanied by an increase in drug resistance.
